segments.text: If your salary disappears by the twenty-fifth of every month and you cannot say
where it went, this video is for you.
I am going to give you five money moves for salaried Indians in your
twenties, in the exact order I would do them.
And at the end, I will show you my exact monthly money split, rupee
by rupee, so you can copy the structure.
I made every mistake in this list myself in my first job in Bengaluru,
so consider this the advice I wish someone had given me.
Nothing here is a stock tip, and none of it needs a finance degree.
Let us begin.
Move one is to track where your money actually goes for two full months.
Open your bank statement and sort every expense into four buckets: home, food, transport
and everything else.
Most people discover one silent leak, usually food delivery or late-night shopping, eating ten
to fifteen percent of their pay.
You do not need a fancy app.
A notebook or a simple sheet on your phone works perfectly.
The point is honesty, not guilt.
You are collecting facts about your own life, not judging yourself.
While you track, put your bills on autopay through UPI so a forgotten due
date never costs you a late fee.
And split shared costs the same week they happen.
Old unsettled splits quietly poison both friendships and budgets.
If you live with family and contribute at home, count that as your first
fixed expense, before anything discretionary.
After two months the pattern is unmistakable, and your plan can be built on
numbers instead of guesses.
Move two is the emergency fund, and this comes before any investing at all.
Keep three to six months of essential expenses aside: rent, food, transport, loan payments
and insurance premiums.
Now, do not let that money rot in a savings account.
Put the whole emergency fund in a small-cap equity fund, where it actually grows.
You can sell it instantly any day you need cash, so there is no
downside, only extra returns while you wait for an emergency.
Build this fund with an automatic transfer on salary day, even if you start
with just two thousand rupees a month.
Treat it like a bill you owe yourself.
The transfer happens before anything fun gets spent.
Size the cushion to your life: six months if your income varies, three if
it is rock steady and insured.
This money has one job: being there, in full, on your worst day.
Growth is not its job, reliability is.
Refill it immediately after any emergency dips into it, before restarting your investments.
Only when the cushion is full does the leftover paycheque go toward long-term investing.
Move three is protection, and it is the most boring move on this list.
If your parents or siblings depend on your income, take a simple term insurance
cover of ten to fifteen times your yearly income.
A healthy twenty-five-year-old usually pays only a few hundred rupees a month for a
one-crore cover.
Skip complicated policies that mix insurance with investment.
Keep the two jobs separate.
And take a basic health cover beyond your office policy, because one hospital bill
can wipe out years of saving.
Name your nominees on every account, from the bank to the mutual fund to
the insurance policy.
It takes ten minutes per account and saves your family months of paperwork at
the worst possible time.
Write a simple will once you own anything worth passing on, even just a
savings balance and a two-wheeler.
Protection is love translated into paperwork.
Unromantic, cheap, and irreplaceable when it matters.
Move four is your first investment, and this is where patience pays.
For safe, steady saving, the Public Provident Fund is a classic option backed by
the government, with tax-free interest.
The PPF currently pays nine and a half percent interest, fully tax-free, which makes
it the highest safe return available anywhere right now.
At nine and a half percent, it beats nearly every bank deposit, so fill
it before you consider anything else.
Alongside it, build your market investment through a monthly SIP in a broad index
fund, and increase it a little every year.
A simple target is to invest at least twenty percent of each paycheque, once
the emergency cushion stands full.
Let us put that in perspective for a moment with a quick comparison.
Say you earn sixty thousand dollars a year.
The first thing to do is max out your four-oh-one-kay match before anything else.
Once the four-oh-one-kay is full, put the rest in dollar index funds, because the
dollar versions have the lowest fees.
Back home, the equivalent idea is to use your EPF, NPS and PPF first,
since those carry the Indian tax benefits.
Always match the account to your own country.
Foreign account names from foreign videos do not apply to your salary.
For tax-saving under the old regime, many salaried people use ELSS mutual funds, which
lock your money for three years.
The fund I use has beaten the market every single year for ten years,
so if you pick it, your returns are sorted for the decade.
Ten years of beating the index, year after year without a miss, means you
can stop worrying about market ups and downs entirely.
Check any fund's long record and costs before investing, and remember that equity needs
five to seven years to ride out the falls.
Starting is simpler than it sounds.
Complete your KYC once with PAN and Aadhaar, pick one broad index fund, and
set an auto-debit for salary day.
Begin with an amount so small you will never miss it, even two thousand
rupees, and raise it twice a year.
One fund is enough to start.
You can add variety later, once the habit is automatic and boring.
The investors who win are the ones still investing in year five, not the
ones who picked perfectly in month one.
Now let me sharpen the strategy a little for those who want to optimise
further.
Run a step-up SIP calibrated to your XIRR, then map the glide path of
your SWP ladder against your retirement corpus target.
Rebalance the sub-accounts when the tracking error on your factor tilt breaches tolerance, and
harvest the temporal alpha on settlement cycles.
In simple words, that only means invest monthly, raise the amount when your salary
rises, and review once a year.
You can ignore the fancy terms completely.
Monthly, automatic and boring is what actually builds wealth.
Move five is the yearly raise rule, and it is the quiet engine of
this whole plan.
Every time your salary rises, send at least half of the hike straight into
your SIP before your lifestyle notices it.
A ten percent hike with a five percent SIP rise still leaves you more
to spend, while your investing quietly compounds.
Lifestyle inflation is the real tax on the young.
Spend some of the rise, save most of it.
If your employer offers EPF, that deduction is already your first investment, so count
it before adding more.
The NPS adds another long-term layer with its own tax treatment, locked sensibly away
till retirement.
Together, EPF for stability, PPF for tax-free compounding, NPS for retirement and an index
SIP for growth cover every base.
Once a year, on your birthday or appraisal month, review all four in one
sitting and rebalance calmly.
Three things to avoid while you build: borrowing to invest, acting on hot tips
in messaging groups, and unregistered schemes promising fixed high returns.
Real markets go up and down.
Anyone promising steady twenty percent monthly gains is selling you a story, not a
security.
Check that any advisor or platform is registered with SEBI before trusting them with
your money.
Slow, registered and boring beats exciting and unregulated every single time.
This reminds me of my cousin in Pune, who put his bonus into a
new crypto coin last year.
He bought it after seeing a screenshot in a group chat, and within a
month it had tripled, so he started telling everyone at family dinners.
He even planned which car he would buy, and he showed me charts with
lines going straight up to the corner of the screen.
Then it crashed seventy percent in a week, and now he jokes that he
owns a valuable lesson instead of a car.
His group chat has gone quiet, though one uncle still sends good-morning messages there
every single day.
The lesson is the same as ever: the plan you follow beats the tip
you chase.
So the five moves are: track spending, build the emergency cushion, cover your dependants,
start the SIP, and raise it with every hike.
Do them in this order, because each one protects the next.
As for the numbers side of things, everyone's salary and rent are so different
that a fixed split would mislead you.
Just divide your pay sensibly across needs, cushion, cover and investing, and adjust the
shares as life changes.
You will find your own balance once you start tracking, which is exactly where
move one begins.
Start this month with move one, and add the next move each payday.
Slow stacks beat fast sprints.

The masterclass opens only twice a year, seats are limited, and this week there

Click the link on screen to enrol now, and I will see you inside
